*letzte*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lest,a contraction of from Middle High German lezzest,from Old High German lezzist (also from Old High German lazzōst),itself superlative of from Old High German laz (cognate to from English late). The modern German form with ''-tz-'' is of northern origin; two separate origins have probably met in it:Firstly,there is a general tendency in some Central German dialects of inserting ''-t-'' before comparative and superlative endings. (Compare for this,for example,Ripuarian from Central Franconian fröh → from Central Franconian fröhter,from Central Franconian fröhtste). Secondly,from Middle Low German lest,contracted superlative of from Middle Low German late,had a regular or regularized variant from Middle Low German letst,which is very rare in writing,but may have been more common in spoken dialects. (Compare modern from German Low German lättst.) Related forms are from Dutch laatst and from Dutch lest,from English latest and from English last,from Luxembourgish lescht,from Hunsrik letst.|Pronunciation}/ˈlɛt͡stə/}Ⓓd/db/De-@^.ogg}letz+te|Adjective}#last}•Das war der '''@^''' Zug.}•That was the last train.}•Er hat seine '''@^''' Freundin betrogen.}•He cheated on his last girlfriend.}#}• Vielleicht träume ich? *Leutnant*German{}|Alternative forms}Leutenant}Lieutenant|Etymology}From Middle French lieutenant; deputy,from French tenir from French le from French lieu from French de (“to keep the position of”). Early on,the form was folk-etymologically reshaped,the first syllable being associated with Leute,the last syllable sometimes with Amt. The normal spoken form in German has been ''Leut(e)nant'' since the 17th century,although the French spelling ''Lieutenant'' remained common and became standard in the 19th century. The contemporary spelling was introduced in the German Empire in 1899 amid rising Franco-German tensions and a general trend of Germanification.|Pronunciation}/ˈlɔʏ̯tnant/}Ⓓa/a7/De-@^.ogg}Leut+nant}Rhymes:ant|Noun}(mask.,plural:[e][@^s][s])}#lieutenant|Usage notes}The normal plural used to be ''@^s''. Today both forms are roughly equally common. The preference seems to depend somewhat on stress patterns,meaning that  is more frequent in the simplex than in compounds.|Derived terms}Generalleutnant}Kapitänleutnant}@^spatent}Oberleutnant

*lieben*German{}|Etymology 1}from Proto-Indo-European idlove}Formally from Middle High German @^,alteration (based on from Middle High German liep) of rarer from Middle High German tto make or be dear,to treat in a friendly way,from Old High German liuben,equivalent to @-2+en.}The singularly attested from Old High German tto love probably remained without continuation; the modern sense was derived in late Middle High German from the noun @-2e on the model of from Middle High German tto love,from Middle High German minne,which had developed a sexual overtone. It remained absent from most traditional dialects,which use variants of @-2 haben or gern haben instead (compare the usage note below). Related to from English love. Compare from Dutch lieven.|Pronunciation}/ˈliːbən/+ˈliːbən+ˈliːbm̩}Ⓓ/6/6d/De-@^2.ogg}Ⓓ/5/52/De-@^.ogg}lie+ben}@-2em some speakers}Rhymes:iːbən|Verb}#usually to love,to have a strong affection for (someone or something)}•Ich '''@-2e''' dich.}•I '''love''' you.}•Ich '''@-2e''' die französische Sprache.}•I '''love''' the French language.}#reflexive to love one another}#reflexive to make love,to have sex|Usage notes}German is more reluctant in its use of ''@^'' (“to love”) than is English,particularly in reference to things. Such phrases as “''Ich @-2e den Teppich in deinem Zimmer!''” (“I love the carpet in your room!”) are a typical feature of “dubbing German”,i.e. literal translations from English as commonly found in dubbed films or sitcoms. A more native way of expressing the same in German would be “''Der Teppich in deinem Zimmer sieht toll aus!''”,or “''Der Teppich in deinem Zimmer gefällt mir sehr gut!''”,or something along these lines.}Even when referring to love between people,''@^'' may have a slightly solemn sound. A more normal way of expressing it in spoken German is @-2 haben,particularly among friends and family,but usually also between lovers. (See the latter lemma for more.)|Adjective}#Form of [@-2]

*liefern*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lieveren (before 1350),which may be borrowed directly from Old French livrer,from Latin līberō,but was probably introduced via from Middle Dutch - and from Middle Low German lēveren (the vocalism ''-ie-'' then being due to hypercorrection; compare also attested ''liebern''). Low German definitely contributed to the spread of the word,which was part of the technical vocabulary of the Hanseatic League. Compare with modern from Dutch leveren,from Swedish leverera and from French livrer.|Pronunciation}/ˈliːfɐn/}Ⓓe/ee/De-@^.ogg}lie+fern|Verb}#transitive to supply,provide @^ ( with  accgoods etc.+:an(acc)to someone/somewhere)}#transitive to deliver (goods,an order,etc.)}#}• Wichtiger ist  dass die Ware innerhalb einer definierten Zeit und an einen genau bestimmten Ort '''geliefert''' wird. *Ludwig*German{}|Alternative forms}Chlodwig|Etymology}From Middle High German Ludewig,from Old High German Ludhuwīg,from Old High German Hludwig,from Old High German ⋆Hlūtwīg,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆Hlūdawīg. The first element is famed; loud (whence modern Cognate German laut),from Proto-Germanic ⋆hlūdaz,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hlūþaz}The name is attested as from Old High German Ludhuwīg in the ''Straßburger Eide'' of 842 (where it contrasts with from Old French Lodhuuig and from Latin Lodhuuic),and as from Old High German Hludwig in the Rhine Franconian Old High German of the ''@^slied'' of 881 (where it contrasts with from Latin Hluduicus). *Maar*German{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}Attested since at least the 16th century,from an underlying from Middle High German ⋆mar(e). Adopted into scientific parlance during the 19th century from gmw-cfr dialects of the Eifel region,home to many maars,which often include the word in their names. The Central Franconian term also has the broader sense of “pool,cesspit,swamp”,which touches on from Middle High German tbog or is even merged with it (cf. from Luxembourgish Muer and from Luxembourgish Mouer). It means "men" as a measure for size or strength of a group rather than individuals:''Mit drei @^ können wir den Schrank heben'' – "With three people we can lift the cupboard." Military or police personnel,team members,demonstrators and the like are often counted using this unchanged plural. This may actually include women.}The plural ''@^en'' is now rare and somewhat poetic. It usually means a group of men,often soldiers,under the command or leadership of someone:''Cäsars @^en'' ("Caesar's men"). *mask.*German{}|Pronunciation}Ⓓe/ee/De-@^.ogg|Adjective}#Abbreviation of [maskulin]}#}'''1926–8''',Leumann–Hofmann–Szantyr,''Lateinische Grammatik'' I:''Lateinische Laut- und Formenlehre'' (2nd ed.,1977),<span style"font-variant:small-caps">Formenlehre Nomen</span> II.B,§ 273:1.d,:}#}:Das Hauptzeugnis für gr. lang+grc+-ειος,der aeol. Gebrauch von patronym. lang:-ειος bei ''o''-Stämmen,ist eine Neuerung; dieses lang:-ειος ist als Universalsuffix auch bei Kons.-Stämmen verwendet; und es stammt als ''-ios''-Ableitung von den Namen auf lang:-ης,so lang:-ειος neben lang:-ης in Thessalien,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης als lang:-εις geschrieben) l. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; auf Lesbos patronym. 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,weibl. 621,11 als Name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; das Muster für '''@^''' lang:-γένειος usw. war vermutlich nicht-patronym. fem. lang:-εια (hom. lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια oder lang:-κλέεια).|The main evidence for Greek lang:-ειος,the Aeolic use of patronymic lang:-ειος with ''o''-stems,is an innovation; this lang:-ειος is used as a universal suffix with consonant stems; and it derives from nouns in lang:-ης as a ''-ios''-derivation,thus lang:-ειος is near lang:-ης in Thessaly,''Schwyzer'',Del. 567 (lang:-ης written as lang:-εις) vid. 80 f. lang:Ἱπποκράτειος,99 f. lang:Ἀντιφάνειος,112 lang:Ἀντιγένειος; patronymic on Lesbos 623,56 lang:Ἱερογένειος,640 lang:Σωγένειος,fem. 621,11 as the name lang:Ἑλλανοκράτεια; the example for the '''masculine''' lang:-γένειος etc. was presumably the non-patronymic fem. lang:-εια (Homeric lang:ἠριγένεια,lang:Ἰφιγένεια,lang:Εὐρύκλεια or lang:-κλέεια).

*Maß*German{}|Alternative forms}Maas}Masz|Etymology}From Middle High German māz,from Old High German māza,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆mātu. Compare from Dutch size,measure,from Mato measure,amount,limit. More at from English mete.}Unrelated to Masse.|Pronunciation}/maːs/}^Ⓓf/f2/De-&_.ogg}Rhymes:aːs}Maas|Noun}(neut.)}#size}#extent}#measure (standard against which something can be judged)}•Ehrlichkeit ist das wahre '''&_''' eines Mannes.}•Honesty is the true '''measure''' of a man.}#}'''1932''',Erich Mühsam,''Die Befreiung der Gesellschaft vom Staat'',in:Erich Mühsam:Prosaschriften II,Verlag europäische ideen Berlin (1978),page 260:}#}:Der Individualismus will umgekehrt den ungekürzten Lebensraum des Individuums zum '''&_''' der gesellschaftlichen Daseinsform machen,ohne Rücksicht auf Gleichheit und Gesamtnutzen.+Individualism,in contrast,wants to make the unshortened living space of the individual the measure of the social form of being,without consideration for equality or total utility.|Usage notes}Most native speakers and even some dictionaries,for example ,confuse this word ('''das &_''') with the rare word ''die &_e'' (plural in all cases:&_en),which is so archaic that it is only used in idiomatic expressions such as these:}in &_en/mit &_en (for example ''in '''&_en''' trinken'' – "to drink in '''moderation'''")}ohne &_en (archaic:sonder &_en)}über alle &_en/über die &_en}In speaking,native speakers nevertheless normally use these idiomatic expressions grammatically correctly with the plural ''&_en''. But when thinking about these expressions and especially while writing,native speakers sometimes use the incorrect form ''&_e'' because they think these idiomatic expressions use the word ''das &_'',whose accusative plural is ''die &_e'' (when in fact these expressions use the word ''die &_e'',whose accusative plural is ''die &_en''). Such was the case in the German Wiktionary until November 2021.}The professionally edited dictionary dwds.de presents these expressions grammatically correctly but does so confusingly without explanation or warning in the entry for ''das &_''. It neither explains why most of these expressions use the form ''&_en'' in the accusative plural nor explains that this is the accusative plural of ''die &_e''. (Expressions with ''mit'' of course use the dative plural,which is the same for both the familiar word ''das &_'' and the rare word ''die &_e''.)|Hyponyms}Ausmaß}Bogenmaß}Ebenmaß}Entfernungsmaß}Flächenmaß}Flüssigkeitsmaß}Gewichtsmaß}Gleichmaß}Gurtmaß}Handelsmaß}Hohlmaß}Holzmaß}Litermaß}Längsmaß}Quermaß}Raummaß}Trockenmaß}Volumenmaß}Versmaß}Winkelmaß}Zuverlässigkeitsmaß|Derived terms}-mäßig}mäßigen}maßgeblich}maßhaltig}mäßig}maßlos}maßstäbig}maßstäblich|Noun}(fem.,plural:[en])}#South Germany a litre/tankard of beer}#}• Rund 230 Schaustellerbetriebe  Gastronomen und Marktkaufleute waren auf dem Wasen dabei. *Meerkatze*German{}2015}right|Etymology}From Middle High German merekatze,from Old High German merikazza (11th century); equivalent to Meer,(sea)Katze,(cat). So called probably because they were brought to Europe over the sea from Africa. The restriction to the specific species is obviously not original,but a fairly recent scientific use. Adelung (ca. 1780) still defines it as referring to any long-tailed monkey. Compare from Middle Dutch meercatte,whence eventually from English meerkat.|Pronunciation}/ˈmeːrˌkatsə/+ˈmeːɐ̯ˌkät͡sə+ˈmɛɐ̯-}Ⓓ8/84/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#guenon Literally:[kind of monkey]}#|Usage notes}Not to be confused with m+:tkind of mongoose,the German word for which is Erdmännchen.|Derived terms}Grüne @^

*mir*Alemannic German{}|Etymology}From from Isthmus Mixe we.|Pronunciation}/&_/(i:stressed/mɪːr/; i:unstressed/mər/)|Pronoun}#personal we}#personal Form of [ich]:(to) me}German|Pronunciation}qualifier:standard/miːɐ̯/}:}Ⓓd/d1/De-&_.ogg}:}Ⓓa/a3/De-&_2.ogg}:}Rhymes:iːɐ̯}qualifier:colloquially in unstressed position/mɐ/+/mə/|Etymology 1}From Isthmus Mixe me,from Isthmus Mixe me,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆miʀ,from Proto-Germanic me,from Proto-Indo-European ⋆(e)me-,from Proto-Indo-European me. More at me,(English).|Pronoun}#personal Form of [ich]:me,to me:}•Er gab es '''&_'''.}•He gave it '''to me'''.}•'''Mir''' ist kalt.|Derived terms}&_s|Etymology 2}From Isthmus Mixe twe. The form originated through assimilation of from Middle High German wir with a preceding verb form and subsequent unetymological segmentation. This is possibly already an from Old High German - development,since a common Old High German ending of the 1st person plural was ''-em'',thus ''bittēm wir'' → ''}bittē-&_'' (modern bitten wir). The contraction as such is definitely old,though the common form of assimilation,both in written Old High German and written Middle High German,is through loss of the nasal:''bittē wir''. The form with ''&_'' may either be a younger development in Middle High German,or a more colloquial form that only later appeared in writing. Older age is suggested by the great dominance of ''&_'' throughout modern dialects of High German. Compare from Yiddish מיר,from Luxembourgish &_. Compare also from Southern Puebla Mixtec twe two,from Norwegian Nynorsk twe.|Pronoun}#dialectal alternative form of [(twe)]}#}'''16th century/1874''',''Alsfelder Passionsspiel mit Wörterbuch herausgegeben von C. W. M. *Mistwetter*German{}|Etymology}Technically a compound of Mist,Wetter,(dung)(weather). ''Mist!'' is a rather common interjection equivalent to from English crap. However,the word is not freely prefixed to nouns,which makes it seem likely that ''@^'' is originally "misty weather",pertaining to from Middle Low German mist. The association with Cognate German dung would thus be secondary. *moin*German{}|Alternative forms}Moin}Moin,Moin (might be perceived as foreign or artificial in some regions,e.g. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern)|Etymology}From,or from the same source as,from German Low German @^,beyond which the etymology is from German not clear; see that entry for more.|Pronunciation}/mɔːɪn/+/mɔːɪŋ/+/mɔɪn/}Ⓓ4/4a/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ3/3f/De-@^2.ogg}Rhymes:ɔːɪn|Interjection}#colloquial hi|Usage notes}Increasingly used outside of Northern Germany.||German Low German{}|Etymology}from German Low German The etymology is not clear.}It stems possibly from moi,from German Low German gml,thus meaning would be '(have a) good one'. This would explain the pronunciation with/ŋ/in some areas,which would stem from regular inflection of from Low German moi.}It is also possible that this word is a borrowing from a from German Low German gmw-fri language,which would explain the vowel sequence/ɔːɪ/,which does not naturally occur in almost any Low German dialect.}Further,many sources say that the word comes from the Berlin area,representing the local pronunciation of from German morning:mɔɐ̯jɘn. The pronunciation would come either from local Low German (where the word was pronounced mɔrʝɘn) and then have undergone r-vocalisation,or from early modern Upper Saxonian (/mɔˤjən/or something similar),which is the German dialect that initially replaced Low German in Berlin. The word was understood as '@^' by the rhotic dialects surrounding the city and spread north from them.}Should this word be a from West Frisian - or Berlinian borrowing,it is likely that it was later conflated with the Low German word ''moi'' (/moːɪ/).}A descent,at least partially,from a lost from German Low German - dialect has also been hypothesized.|Pronunciation}/mɔːɪn/}/mɔːɪŋ/|Interjection}#informal hi

*Mord*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German mort,from Old High German mord,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆morþ,from Proto-Germanic ⋆murþą. (Murder is)  as known to every educated prosecutor  an act that is committed in utmost ecstasy and with the coldest brutality.|Usage notes}Certain milder cases of murder,such as the American second-degree murder,are often covered by Totschlag in German legal terminology and do not then qualify as ''@^.''}An English phrase like “''Peter's murder''” is ambiguous as it can mean either “the murder that Peter committed” or “the murder by which Peter was killed”. In German,„''Peters @^''” can only mean the former. *muffig*German{}|Etymology}The senses "smelly" and "grumpy" go back to different origins. The former pertains to Muff from Middle Low German muffen; the latter to Muffel,which is an Upper German dialect word of unknown origin. In contemporary German both senses often overlap (see below). It is therefore impossible to treat them as separate words anymore. *Muttern*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈmʊtərn/+ˈmʊtɐn}Ⓓ6/61/De-@^.ogg|Noun}#Form of [@-1]|Noun}#archaic Form of [@-1]|Usage notes}The dialectal inflected form '''''@^''''' is (or was) applied in the dative and accusative cases when used without an article,i.e. in the sense of “mum”:''Du sollst @-1'''n''' helfen.'' — “You're supposed to help Mum.” This was typical of eastern German dialects,including that of Berlin,but is now widely obsolete. A remnant of this is the phrase wie bei @^,which is in general use.
